input:
The pressure drop values that have been reported for the benchmark material by the two groups differ considerably, and it is important to consider the reasons for this difference before any preference between the two sets of values can be established. It should be noted that the difference between the two sets is larger than the scatter that either group reports within its own runs, which suggests that the difference is a systematic one rather than a matter of measurement error.

On closer examination, it appears that the two groups did not in fact measure the material under the same conditions. One group carried out its measurements on a bed that had been packed for the test and was used in that state, whereas the other group carried out its measurements after the bed had been subjected to repeated adsorption and regeneration cycles, and it is the second group that reports the higher values. This is perhaps not surprising, because a bed that has been cycled is no longer the same as a freshly packed bed: the particles are worked against one another, fines are generated and migrate into the void spaces, and the passages available for the gas become narrower, so that a higher pressure drop is only to be expected.

It would therefore seem reasonable to prefer the values obtained on the cycled bed, provided that the duty under consideration does in fact involve cycling of the same kind. Where the bed is to be packed, used once and replaced, the fresh-bed values would be the more appropriate set, and on balance the preference depends on the condition of the bed in service rather than on any judgement about the quality of the measurements themselves.
target:
For the benchmark material, the two reported sets of pressure drop values stand apart by more than either group reports as scatter within its own runs, and the gap follows the test conditions rather than the material. One group measured on a bed packed for the test and used as packed. The other measured after the bed had been through repeated adsorption and regeneration, and its values are the higher of the two. A cycled bed is not the bed that was packed: cycling works the particles against each other, fines form and migrate into the voids, and the passages the gas sees are narrower than those of the fresh packing, so a higher pressure drop at the same duty is what the bed's state predicts, not an anomaly in either measurement.

Read on that basis, the two sets are not in conflict about the material. They describe the benchmark material in two states of the bed, and the apparent disagreement is a difference in what was actually put under test. The cycled values also carry a condition the fresh values do not: the fresh state can be reproduced at will, while the cycled state depends on the whole cycling history, and that history has to travel with the numbers wherever they are quoted.

The preference here is for the cycled-bed values, on one stated condition: that the duty under consideration cycles the bed in the same way. For a bed that is packed, used once and replaced, the fresh-bed values are the relevant set and the preference reverses. Neither set is set aside as a measurement failure, and the error lies in taking a design figure from the wrong state.
